items.q: You should build a simple baseline model before trying complex ones because…
choices: It sets a bar complexity must beat and exposes data problems cheaply
items.explain: A baseline you must deliberately beat exposes label errors, leakage, and weak features before you spend weeks tuning.

items.q: A feature computed from data timestamped after the prediction moment is…
choices: Target leakage: information from the future the model will not have live
items.explain: If the feature cannot exist at prediction time, the training score is fiction and production performance collapses.

items.q: The correct place to fit preprocessing (scalers, encoders) is…
choices: Inside the pipeline, fit on training folds only
On the test set for accuracy
items.explain: Fitting on all data leaks test statistics into training. Pipelines fit preprocessing per training fold, keeping the estimate honest.

items.q: For a fraud model where missing a fraud costs 50x a false alarm, you optimize…
choices: Recall (or a cost-weighted metric), not accuracy
items.explain: The metric must match the business cost: on asymmetric costs, accuracy rewards the majority-class constant predictor.

items.q: Logging model inputs and predictions in production primarily enables…
choices: Auditing, debugging, and detecting drift after deployment
items.explain: Logged predictions are the raw material for drift detection, error analysis, and retraining decisions.

items.q: A shadow deployment means…
choices: The new model scores live traffic in parallel without affecting responses, for comparison
items.explain: Shadow mode validates the new model on real traffic safely before it takes over decision-making.

items.q: The strongest portfolio signal from an applied ML project is…
choices: A clear problem, honest held-out evaluation with limits stated, and a working demo
items.explain: Perfect scores signal leakage or toy problems; honest evaluation with stated limits signals an engineer.

items.q: Gradient boosting differs from random forests fundamentally in that it…
choices: Trains trees sequentially, each correcting the previous ensemble's errors
items.explain: Boosting is sequential error correction; bagging (forests) averages independent trees to cut variance.

items.q: A well-calibrated classifier's predicted probability of 0.7 means…
choices: It is 70% confident in a vague sense
Among cases scored 0.7, about 70% are actually positive
It will be right 70% of the time overall
items.explain: Calibration is the match between stated probabilities and observed frequencies — checkable on a reliability diagram.

items.q: Adam's main practical advantage over plain SGD is…
choices: It always finds the global optimum
Adaptive per-parameter learning rates that usually converge faster with less tuning
It needs no learning rate at all
items.explain: Adam adapts step sizes per parameter from gradient history — robust and fast in practice, though SGD+momentum can generalize slightly better with care.

items.q: Stacking base-model predictions as features for a meta-model risks…
choices: Leakage, unless base predictions come from out-of-fold estimates
items.explain: Training the meta-model on in-sample base predictions leaks; out-of-fold predictions keep the stack honest.

items.q: Entity embeddings for high-cardinality categoricals help because they…
choices: Learn dense representations capturing similarity between categories
items.explain: Embeddings place similar categories near each other in a learned space — far more expressive than one-hot for thousands of levels.

items.q: A learning-rate warmup (small LR rising to target) primarily addresses…
choices: Early-training instability from large initial gradients
items.explain: Starting small lets the optimizer settle before taking full-size steps — standard practice in deep training.

items.q: An ablation study in your project tells a reviewer…
choices: Which components actually contributed, by measuring performance with each removed
items.explain: Remove each piece and measure the drop: honest credit assignment for architecture and feature decisions.

items.q: In NumPy, a (3,1) array added to a (4,) array broadcasts to…
items.explain: Broadcasting aligns trailing dimensions: (3,1) with (4,) becomes (3,4).

items.q: df.groupby('city')['price'].mean() computes…
items.explain: groupby splits rows by city, then the aggregation collapses each group to its mean price.

items.q: Vectorized NumPy code beats Python loops mainly because…
choices: The loop runs in compiled C over contiguous memory
NumPy uses the GPU by default
items.explain: Vectorized ops execute in optimized C on contiguous buffers — often 10-100x faster than interpreted loops.

items.q: train_test_split exists to…
choices: Hold out unseen data so evaluation measures generalization
items.explain: Evaluating on data the model never trained on is the only honest estimate of future performance.

items.q: A histogram with a long right tail tells you the distribution is…
choices: Right-skewed: a few large values pull the mean above the median
items.explain: Right skew means rare large values; the mean exceeds the median and some models need transforms.

items.q: In scikit-learn, fit() then predict() means…
choices: Learn parameters from training data, then apply to new data
items.explain: fit learns from the training set; predict applies the learned mapping to unseen inputs — the whole API in two verbs.

items.q: The KV cache in transformer inference exists to…
choices: Avoid recomputing key/value projections for past tokens during generation
items.explain: Autoregressive generation reuses cached K/V for previous tokens; the cache is why long contexts cost memory.

items.q: LoRA fine-tuning works by…
choices: Training small low-rank adapter matrices while freezing the base model
items.explain: LoRA injects trainable low-rank updates into frozen weights — most of the adaptation at a fraction of the cost.

items.q: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) differs from RLHF mainly in that it…
choices: Optimizes preferences directly without training a separate reward model + RL loop
items.explain: DPO turns preference pairs into a direct loss — simpler than the reward-model-then-PPO pipeline, with its own tradeoffs.

items.q: The biggest methodological risk of LLM-as-judge evaluation is…
choices: Bias: judges favor verbosity, their own style, and position — and can be gamed
items.explain: LLM judges carry systematic biases and can be optimized against; they complement but never replace task-grounded evals.

items.q: Quantizing a model from 16-bit to 4-bit primarily trades…
choices: Memory and speed against small quality degradation
items.explain: Lower precision shrinks memory and speeds inference; quality loss is usually small but must be measured on your task.

items.q: Instruction tuning helps a base model mainly by…
choices: Teaching the response format and behavior expected, more than new facts
items.explain: SFT teaches the model how to respond — format, tone, instruction-following — on top of pretraining's knowledge.

items.q: A GenAI regression suite should run…
choices: On every model or prompt change, comparing against pinned expected behaviors
items.explain: Models and prompts drift; pinned golden cases catch regressions before users do.

items.q: Aggressive text normalization (lowercasing, stemming, stopword removal) before a modern transformer classifier is…
choices: Usually unnecessary or harmful: subword models use full context
items.explain: Contextual models learn from the full sequence; bag-of-words-era normalization now mostly destroys signal.

items.q: In NER evaluation, the standard metric is…
items.explain: Entity recognition is scored on exact spans with correct types; token accuracy is inflated by the easy non-entity majority.

items.q: Cosine similarity over sentence embeddings is useful for…
choices: Semantic search: finding texts close in meaning
items.explain: Embeddings place similar meanings near each other; cosine similarity turns that geometry into search and clustering.

items.q: The binding constraint on most production NLP systems is…
items.explain: No architecture outruns bad labels; annotation quality and coverage usually cap performance before modeling choices do.

items.q: Using an LLM to label training data requires…
choices: A quality audit: sample labels checked against human judgment, with disagreement analysis
items.explain: LLM labels are cheap but biased; auditing a sample against human labels tells you whether the cheap labels are usable.

items.q: Chunking long documents before embedding exists because…
choices: Models have context limits and long texts dilute the representation; chunks keep retrieval precise
items.explain: One vector per 50-page document buries specifics; chunking keeps each embedding focused so retrieval finds the right passage.

items.q: Structured output (JSON schemas) from an LLM primarily gives you…
choices: A parseable contract: the model fills typed fields your code can trust structurally
items.explain: Schemas turn free text into data your program can consume — validation still required, but parsing stops being the failure point.

items.q: Reranking in a RAG pipeline exists to…
choices: Improve precision: reorder retrieved candidates so the best passages reach the prompt
items.explain: Retrieval optimizes recall cheaply; a reranker spends more compute on the top candidates to fix ordering.

items.q: A golden dataset for an AI feature is…
choices: A curated set of representative cases with expected behaviors, run as regression tests
items.explain: Golden cases pin expected behavior; running them on every prompt or model change catches regressions before users do.

items.q: The honest UX for an uncertain AI answer includes…
choices: Citations, confidence signals, and an easy correction path
items.explain: Users calibrate trust from signals: show sources, signal uncertainty, and make corrections cheap.

items.q: Caching LLM responses is primarily a…
choices: Cost and latency control for repeated or similar queries
items.explain: Deterministic or repeated prompts should not burn tokens twice; caching is the cheapest optimization in the stack.

items.q: An AI feature's biggest production risk is usually…
choices: Unbounded behavior: no guardrails, no evals, no cost limits around a nondeterministic component
items.explain: Nondeterministic components need deterministic scaffolding: evals, guardrails, budgets — or the feature is a liability.

items.q: The first question before any applied AI project should be…
choices: Is ML actually the answer — could rules, heuristics, or an existing product solve it?
How big the model should be
items.explain: The honest checklist kills doomed projects early: many ‘AI problems’ are search, rules, or buyable products.

items.q: Defining success metrics before modeling matters because…
choices: It prevents optimizing a metric nobody cares about and gives the project a finish line
items.explain: A model optimized for the wrong metric is a successful failure; the metric is the contract with the business.

items.q: Weak supervision (heuristic labeling functions) is useful when…
choices: Labeling budget is small: noisy programmatic labels bootstrap a first model
items.explain: Heuristics generate large noisy label sets cheaply; a model trained on them often beats hand-labeling a tiny set.

items.q: A Wizard-of-Oz prototype for an AI feature means…
choices: A human simulates the AI behind a realistic interface to test the concept before building the model
items.explain: Test whether users want the capability at all before investing in the model — the cheapest validation available.

items.q: Human-in-the-loop in production is best framed as…
choices: A design choice: humans handle the uncertain cases the model flags, improving both safety and labels
items.explain: Routing low-confidence cases to humans is a feature: safer decisions now, and the reviewed cases become training data.

items.q: The pre-launch review for an AI system should put on the table…
choices: Known failure modes, limits, monitoring plan, and rollback criteria
items.explain: Risks named before launch become monitored metrics; risks discovered after launch become incidents.
